Nor is Britain unusually generous by European standards. The OECD estimates a net pension replacement rate of 44.7 percent for an average UK earner, compared with 54.5 percent across the EU27. The figures are substantially higher in countries including Spain, Portugal and Sweden. Pension systems differ, of course, but Britain hardly has an extravagant state pension by any standard.

This is fundamentally a debate about inequality, although you wouldn’t know it from the headlines. In England, healthy life expectancy in the most deprived areas is just 49.8 years for men and 48.2 years for women, compared with 69.2 and 68.5 years in the least deprived areas. Since 2019–21, healthy life expectancy has fallen in the most deprived areas.

Behind those statistics are people who have spent their lives in low-paid and physically demanding work, often in poorer housing and with worse health. They are not simply dying sooner; many are also reaching later life with greater needs and fewer resources.

These are the generations who lived through the war and helped rebuild Britain in its wake. They contributed to the society from which all of us have benefited. To treat them as a convenient source of savings, as the government is now proposing, is to deny them the dignity and security they deserve.

There is much to agree with in the proposed National Care Service. The principle is a straightforward social democratic one: if someone becomes frail or needs help in their daily life, access to care should not depend on their savings or whether they own their home. Britain is one of the richest countries in the world. We can afford this without a raid on the elderly.

The current £84 billion tax relief on pension payments is heavily skewed towards those with higher incomes. The more you earn, the more relief you receive, and so the bigger your pension. Even more striking is that the rich can shelter assets in their pension funds which can grow substantially over a working lifetime, with no need to pay capital gains tax on them. The pensions setup in the UK is nothing less than a scam by the rich. Why not help pay for the National Care Service by correcting this grossly unfair distribution?

The NHS does not tell cancer patients that they must first spend their life savings before receiving treatment. It pools risk and provides care according to need. So let’s do the same with care, making it a right rather than a commodity. We don’t have to set the young against the old or taxpayers against pensioners. These zero-sum decisions are the stuff of the neoliberal economics that Burnham claims to oppose. A decent pension and free personal care are both possible with a progressive tax system. The left must push the government to build one.

entry.summary: Britain doesn’t have to choose between a decent pension and decent care. We can — and should — provide both.

entry.title: The UK Is Failing Palestinians At Home and Abroad

div.p: For Palestinians arriving in Britain after surviving Israel’s genocide in Gaza, crossing the border does not mean the end of the crisis. It means entering a new struggle for safety.

Their trauma moves with them. Spouses, children, parents and siblings may still be in Gaza. They continue to receive messages from relatives describing bombardment, starvation and the destruction around them. They wait for news of loved ones whose safety they cannot guarantee. They try to build a life in Britain while knowing that their families remain trapped in a territory annihilated by genocide.

Yet the British state treats their arrival as a standard immigration and administrative matter, as though the genocide ceases to exist in their lives once they are in the UK. Newly arrived Palestinians are forced to navigate the UK’s increasingly hostile immigration environment on their own, resulting in acute housing insecurity and insufficient mental health support as they struggle to recover from years of devastation. At the same time, the government continues to prevent spouses, parents, and children from reuniting, ensuring that the suffering of Palestinian families continues across borders.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s decision to restart the refugee resettlement scheme with a focus on Palestinians is progress. But it still falls far short of the scale of action that’s urgently needed amidst an ongoing genocide in which the UK itself is complicit. If this government is serious about rectifying Keir Starmer’s failures on Palestine, it needs to confront all of the policies that harm Palestinian lives — both abroad and here in Britain.

There’s no official figure for the number of Palestinians who have arrived in Britain from Gaza since October 2023, but community data estimates the number to be around 2,000 people. In this time, Palestinians have entered the country through student visas, refugee family reunion (before its suspension), medical evacuation, and irregular routes, rather than through a dedicated scheme to quickly get Palestinians to safety.

The Ukraine Family Scheme, on the other hand, was introduced less than ten days after Russia’s invasion in 2022 to allow Ukrainians to flee violence and join their family members in Britain. The scheme recognised that ordinary immigration procedures were inadequate and provided a route designed around the realities of war. By the time it closed in February 2024, the government had granted nearly 75,000 visas for family reunion, in addition to over 200,000 visas through the Homes for Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme.

Three years into the genocide in Gaza, there’s still no specific family route allowing Palestinians in Britain to temporarily bring their relatives in Gaza to safety. Such a scheme would only make around 5,000 Palestinians eligible for reunification, a figure that pales in comparison to the number of people who came to the UK through tailored routes from Ukraine, Afghanistan and Hong Kong.

Palestinian families are instead expected to navigate immigration routes designed for entirely different circumstances. The situation became even more difficult after then Home Secretary Yvette Cooper suspended the refugee family reunion route in September 2025, removing one of the few available paths for the reunification of refugees in Britain with their spouses and children abroad.

This decision has had a direct impact on Palestinian families, including for those who had already applied. In July, The Guardian reported that the Home Office has been blocking dozens of women and children in Gaza from reuniting with an immediate family member who has refugee status in the UK. Even though they had applied before route’s suspension, the Home Office has used legal challenges to actively prevent their evacuation and has even claimed that their small children pose a security risk to Britain. In response, a Home Office spokesperson simply said, ‘Under our reforms to create a fairer asylum system, family reunion will no longer be automatic. Those seeking to bring family members to the UK will need to meet stricter criteria’. Home Secretary Mahmood has not provided further explanation.

Yesterday, however, Mahmood announced that the Home Office will reopen the UK Resettlement Scheme, a different route that operates in partnership with the UN Refugee Agency, with twenty five per cent of arrivals to be Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. While this is a welcome development, the total number of people to arrive under the scheme will initially be in the hundreds and may only rise to thousands at some point in the future. Palestinians will make up less than a quarter of these refugees. This is not an adequate response to the demands of Palestinians in the UK who desperately want to bring their families to safety.

But even when Palestinians in Gaza are eligible for travel to the UK, they can face an impossible bureaucratic barrier: biometrics. The UK Visa Application Centre in Gaza has been closed since October 2023 due to Israel’s bombardment. Applicants are therefore expected to travel elsewhere to provide their fingerprints and photo, but Palestinians living under siege can’t simply travel to another country to complete their visa application. Rather than finding an alternative, the government has left them in Gaza, struggling to survive.

Of course, there is already a mechanism within the immigration system for dealing with exceptional circumstances, one which makes it possible to excuse an applicant from providing biometrics before travelling to the UK. Under the Ukraine scheme, for example, biometrics were taken upon arrival in the UK. This is also the arrangement for the small number of people who managed to leave Gaza through the UK’s medical evacuation and scholarship arrangements. In these cases, the Home Office conducts security checks using biographical information before departure, while visa processing and biometric enrolment are coordinated after people have exited Gaza with Foreign Office support.

A dedicated Gaza Family Scheme operating under this model would enable the Home Office to conduct the necessary eligibility and security checks while allowing eligible applicants who cannot access a visa application centre to provide their biometrics after leaving Gaza or reaching the UK. Once the Home Office has approved an application, the Foreign Office could then facilitate the person’s evacuation from Gaza and onward travel to Britain.
This is not a question of precedent or policy know-how; it’s a question of political will.

When Palestinians do enter the UK, they arrive having survived bombardment, starvation, forced displacement, the destruction of their homes and communities, and the loss of family members. Some have spent months or years moving between shelters, living without adequate food, clean water or healthcare, while watching their neighbourhoods disappear around them.

Yet even the few Palestinians who receive refugee or humanitarian protection are quickly forced back into housing insecurity and destitution. The British Palestinian Committee, where I work as a Senior Community Advocacy Officer, has documented several cases of Palestinians becoming homeless after receiving protection from the state since 2023.

One Palestinian man with serious physical and mental health needs was placed in unsuitable accommodation after receiving humanitarian protection. After being admitted to hospital, he returned to find that he had been refused entry to his accommodation because he had been absent. He was left homeless for five days, relying on emergency support from voluntary organisations. In Manchester, two Palestinian brothers were left homeless after being required to leave Home Office accommodation. Both approached the local authority for assistance but were ultimately left without stable housing.

The private rental market offers little relief. Refugees are expected to provide deposits, rent in advance, guarantors, references and proof of income — precisely the things that people don’t have immediately after surviving a genocide. Some Palestinians have been forced to borrow money from friends and community members simply to secure accommodation.

Palestinian refugees are also forced to navigate Universal Credit, banking, employment, and healthcare with little to no support. This is not successful integration, it’s precarity imposed on people who’ve already experienced catastrophic loss.
Housing has a direct impact on mental health. As one young Palestinian told the BPC, ‘How can I ask for therapy when I’m sleeping on the street, and my family is in a tent after our home was bombed?’

In 2025, the BPC conducted a six-month mental health programme, which mapped available mental health resources, supported access to care, and delivered community-based activities for newly arrived Palestinians. We found that mental health needs among Palestinians arriving in Britain are widespread, severe and frequently unmet.

The trauma experienced by Palestinians is cumulative and it continues even if a Palestinian is physically safe in Manchester or London, but their children remain in danger in Gaza. ‘I don’t have the luxury of thinking about my mental health. My wife and children are still trapped in Gaza and I still can’t bring them to safety” one Palestinian man told me. Newfound immigration and housing insecurity only exacerbate the situation.

The NHS has an essential role to play in supporting survivors of genocide, but Palestinians also suffer from the general crisis of mental health infrastructure across the UK. They are forced to endure long wait times, the absence of trauma-informed early intervention pathways, limited culturally and linguistically appropriate provision, and Britain’s failures to meaningfully integrate mental health services with housing, immigration, and welfare systems.
Yet even if care provision were perfect, no therapist can reunite a parent separated from a child trapped in Gaza, and no prescription can provide someone with a home.

Earlier this month, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband acknowledged that ‘the most unimaginable trauma and suffering in the last three years — death, destruction and dehumanisation on an appalling scale’ has been perpetrated against Gaza. He announced the start of a new approach ‘that not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts’.
But will these words mean anything for the Palestinians who arrive to the UK, or for their spouses and children waiting to be brought to safety?

Family reunification, secure housing, meaningful access to healthcare and a serious mental health response would be a start. These are not demands for preferential treatment. They are demands for a system capable of responding to exceptional circumstances — circumstances that the UK itself helped create.

entry.summary: Palestinians arriving from Gaza face homelessness, mental health crises and a Home Office actively restricting family reunion.

entry.title: Trade Unionists to Burnham: End Military Collaboration With Saudi Arabia

p.i: After Andy Burnham’s announcement earlier this week that the UK would continue to give military support to Saudi Arabia as it reignites its war on Yemen, ten of the country’s leading trade unionists came together to oppose this reckless decision, which will deepen the suffering of the region’s people. Here is their letter in full:

div.p: Dear Prime Minister,

As trade union leaders we are shocked by the government’s decision to provide yet more military support to Saudi Arabia. Britain should not collaborate with a military that has repeatedly violated international law and has been central to creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises in Yemen.

Providing military support to Saudi Arabia inflames the war started by the US and Israel against Iran in February, which has expanded across the region. Contrary to the government’s statements, the more this war expands, the more expensive our bills will get. The only way out is a diplomatic settlement to the regional war.

Saudi Arabia has intervened in Yemen for 11 years, with devastating results. Throughout this war, the Saudi-led coalition has repeatedly targeted civilians, breaking international law, while its air and sea blockade helped cause a humanitarian crisis that left 377,000 people dead by 2021. Britain has supported this war throughout — supplying Saudi Arabia with aircraft, missiles and on-the-ground maintenance to keep its fighter jets in the sky. Earlier this year, the government approved a £468 million weapons sale to Saudi Arabia, mostly composed of missiles. These actions have fuelled a brutal war that has left Yemen in ruins. Providing military support to Saudi Arabia as the US-Iran war extends to Yemen only exacerbates regional conflict and takes us further from the diplomatic settlement that the world urgently needs.

As the war expands, our members are paying the price. Inflation rose again in August, driven by petrol prices. Energy bills will rise again in October, perhaps exceeding £2100 for the average household from January. Escalating this war will make our bills more expensive. If the government is serious about tackling the cost of living crisis, it must get serious about diplomacy.

First, we ask you to urgently end Britain’s military support for Saudi Arabia. Second, we ask you to end the UK’s wider involvement in the Iran war, by revoking support for US air strikes launched from RAF bases. These are essential steps for a cost-of-living government to take.
Yours sincerely,
Andrea Egan, General Secretary, UNISON
Daniel Kebede, General Secretary, National Education Union
Dave Ward, General Secretary, Communication Workers Union
Eddie Dempsey, General Secretary, National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers
Fran Heathcote, General Secretary, Public and Commercial Services Union
Jo Grady, General Secretary, University and College Union
Paul W. Fleming, General Secretary, Equity
Maryam Eslamdoust, General Secretary, Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association
Sarah Woolley, General Secretary, Bakers, Food and Allied Workers’ Union
Steve Wright, General Secretary, Fire Brigades Union

entry.summary: Ten of the country's leading unions tell the government to end support for the war on Yemen.

entry.title: Israel’s Accountability Theatre

div.p: On the 19th of August, 933 days after the five-year-old Palestinian Hind Rajab was murdered, the Israeli army decided to open an investigation.

When Hind’s murder became global news, the world listened to the horrifying audio recording of a terrified child begging Palestinian paramedics to save her. We then learned that the paramedics sent to rescue her were killed too.

The Israeli military initially claimed that its forces were not even at the scene. Months later, it refined this position in a preliminary review: Israeli soldiers, it said, were ‘not present near the vehicle or within firing range’ of the car in which Hind, her aunt, her uncle and her four cousins were trapped.

That denial fell apart after sustained outside pressure, which came in part from The Voice of Hind Rajab, a film built around the real recordings of her final calls, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival in 2025. It also came from quality journalism: a joint investigation by Al Jazeera and The Hind Rajab Foundation placed an Israeli tank as close as 13 metres from the vehicle, well within view of the seven civilians. Only once that pressure had built for two and a half years did the Israeli military admit, on August 19, 2026, that its soldiers had fired on the car.

The Israeli military has designed the perfect sequence to protect itself from real accountability, while using selective investigations and admissions to deal with international condemnation. Its last comparable high-profile admission was over the killing of Al Jazeera correspondent Shireen Abu Akleh in 2022. At first the Israeli military attempted to shift the blame to a Palestinian gunmen, before mounting evidence and multiple investigations forced it to concede a ‘high probability’ that one of its own soldiers fired the fatal shot. The Military Advocate General ruled that the case did not meet the threshold for a criminal investigation, however, and closed the file before it a suspect was named.

That is the phase that Hind Rajab’s case is now entering. A review by Action on Armed Violence of 52 publicly reported Israeli military probes into incidents in Gaza and the West Bank found that 88 percent had either closed with no finding of wrongdoing or simply stayed open indefinitely, with no outcome ever made public. Since October 2023, despite the clear evidence of Israeli soldiers exterminating Palestinians, nearly 100 deaths of Palestinian detainees in Israeli military custody, and widespread documentation of Israeli soldiers looting Palestinian homes, there has only been a single conviction. Israel recently declined to open any investigation into three other notable lethal incidents, including the April 2024 killing of seven aid workers including 3 British Nationals John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby. In 2024, far right protesters, including sitting lawmakers, broke into the Sde Teiman base to try to stop military police from detaining reservists who sexually abused a Palestinian detainee. National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir publicly backed the soldiers, calling their detention ‘shameful’.

Even rare victories for ‘accountability’ tend to crumble on contact with Israeli politics. Elor Azaria, an army medic, shot Abdel Fattah al-Sharif, a wounded Palestinian, in the head as he lay motionless on the ground in Hebron in 2016. The shooting was captured on video. Despite pressure from right-wing politicians and protesters, Gadi Eisenkot, then chief of staff of the Israeli military, insisted Azaria stand trial. Eisenkot is now the leading challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election this October. Azaria was convicted of manslaughter in 2017 and sentenced to 18 months. Then Eisenkot himself cut that to 14. A parole board cut it again, to nine. Azaria walked free in May 2018 and was carried through the streets on his supporters’ shoulders as a hero. In July 2026, the same summer the IDF was quietly reviewing the Hind Rajab file, Israel’s own defense minister, Israel Katz, formally asked the president to expunge Azaria’s criminal record entirely, saying the conviction sent an unfair message to ‘our sons and daughters’ in uniform.

Taken together, these cases describe a system built to adapt to international pressure when it becomes necessary to protect Israel’s credibility with Western governments, while avoiding any real action against soldiers accused of abuse. Investigations are opened for their PR value and admissions are timed to relieve diplomatic pressure rather than to establish facts. This serves two purposes at once: it lets Israel off the hook with foreign governments, and it assures soldiers, and the public, that the army will protect them no matter what violence they inflict on Palestinians. Given that Israel’s ongoing state of war depends on a steady flow of soldiers willing to serve, that second message matters more than the first.
There is no doubt that Israel will try to repeat this same procedure with the newly opened Hind Rajab investigation. Whether it succeeds depends on the scale of the pressure we can apply.

entry.summary: The Zionist entity is stage-managing its military investigations to protect professional killers from justice.

entry.title: In Sweden, the Far Right is a Victim of its Own Success

div.p: A few weeks ago, polls were predicting a comfortable win for the left in Sweden’s general elections. But when the ballot was held on 13 September it returned a knife-edge result, one that was too close to call for several days. It was finally announced that the left bloc, led by the Social Democrats, had won 176 seats in the Riksdag to the right’s 173 — a margin of just over 50,000 votes. Though it looks like the Social Democrats will lead the next government, this will go down as the party’s worst electoral performance since the introduction of universal suffrage in 1918.

Few are happy with the outcome. While the Social Democrats’ loss in terms of overall vote share was made up for by the combined gains of the three other parties that make up the left bloc — the Left, the Greens and the Centre — these smaller formations don’t have much to celebrate either. At least not yet. To translate their new votes into power over policy, they must first reach an agreement both with the Social Democrats and with each other. That may prove difficult, especially for the Left and the Centre, whose economic policies often tend towards opposite ends of the spectrum. The Left has insisted they will not support any government in which they aren’t included, while the Centre has ruled out supporting any government that includes the Left. It falls to the leader of the Social Democrats, Magdalena Andersson, to get them to come to an agreement.

Meanwhile, Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing coalition which ruled for the past four years has been booted out, but not nearly as decisively as the left had hoped. Kristersson’s Moderate party advanced slightly, while the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) — on whom his government has been heavily reliant — lost 3 percent of the vote share compared with 2022, shrinking to 17.5 percent. In an election with only small vote swings, this was the single biggest loss of any party, and the first time the SD’s seat share has diminished since they entered parliament in 2010. The smaller parties in the right wing bloc, the Liberals and the Christian Democrats, saw modest increases, but not enough to offset the far right’s decline.

Over the past four years, the SD has been a ‘collaboration partner’ of the Kristersson government, supporting it without being an official member of the coalition. In 2022, the SD signed an agreement (‘Tidöavtalet’) with the Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals, in which it gave up any formal government role in exchange for wide-ranging influence over several policy areas, including immigration and crime. While some commentators described this as an enviable position — SD wielded enormous power without governing responsibility — the reality is somewhat different. In the eyes of the public, the SD may as well have been part of the government, so obvious was its impact on policy. As a result, the party has had to navigate the inevitable difficulties involved in supporting an already unwieldy three-party coalition, and voters have held it accountable for the less popular parts of the government’s programme.

Despite the far right’s dropoff, its election campaign proved that the party has now been normalised within the Swedish political landscape. As its leader Jimmie Åkesson told members after the polls closed on Sunday, the SD may have lost some votes, but what they have gained over the past four years, as collaborators of the Kristersson government, is a level of respectability that was previously unthinkable. Their representatives are no longer a maligned and untouchable group within the Riksdag, their voters no longer ashamed of their affiliation. For a party with roots in the neo-Nazi movement, there was no guarantee that this detoxification would succeed. But now, for the first time ever, the Sweden Democrats have campaigned alongside the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals as equal partners in a unified team. No demands were made that they be kept out of a future governing coalition.

The party has not needed to water down its policies or rhetoric to achieve this normalisation. It campaigned on the slogan ‘Make Sweden Sweden Again’ and insisted that the participation of Sweden’s Muslim and immigrant population in the political process, skewing the results in favour of the left, was an urgent problem in itself.

Ironically, one of the reasons for the party’s poor performance in this election may be that it has already had huge success remaking Sweden in its image. Over the past four years, the SD have been so adept at bending politics to their will that some of their previous voters appear to think that their reforms have now gone far enough, or even too far.

Since the Kristersson government came to power, Sweden has done a decisive U-turn on immigration policy (which began as a series of temporary measures introduced by the Social Democrats in response to the migration crisis of 2015), while systematically overhauling its criminal justice system. The coalition has made temporary rather than permanent residence permits the default for asylum-seekers and severely restricted the possibility of family reunification. It has curtailed the possibility of being granted asylum on humanitarian grounds, hiked salary thresholds for work visas, and severely reduced the number of refugees accepted via third-country resettlement schemes. It has introduced laws requiring public officials to report suspected illegal immigrants, given the police increased powers to carry out internal immigration controls, and made it possible to deny or revoke residence permits, not just for those convicted of crimes, but also for people who have shown ‘bristande vandel’ — meaning, roughly, a ‘lack of good conduct’ (a standard which legal experts warn is just as arbitrary as it sounds). Paths to Swedish citizenship have been restricted, and, to add insult to injury, the government has introduced voluntary repatriation grants of around £26,500 for immigrants to permanently leave Sweden.

In the sphere of criminal justice and policing, the reforms are just as extensive. Longer and tougher sentences have been introduced for a wide range of crimes, and the government has reduced or removed rules relating to more lenient sentencing for offenders under 21. The age of criminal responsibility has been lowered from 15 to 14, and the rules governing court procedures have been changed to allow for anonymous witnesses as well as Crown witnesses. Police have been given unprecedented new powers — including, in terminology by now familiar to all Swedes, ‘secretive and preventative coercive methods’, which can be used against adults and children alike, whether or not they are suspected of any crime. Police have also been given the power to temporarily designate certain areas as ‘visitation zones’, where they can stop and search anyone they please.

It would have been easier for the left to make a strong case against the record of the Kristersson government, and the deep damage it has done to longstanding legal and democratic principles, were it not for two uncomfortable facts. First, the swerve in immigration policy, as well as parts of the criminal justice reforms, have been incredibly popular. (So deep is the shift in the political landscape that the Social Democrats, too, now accept many of these reforms and are unlikely to reverse course.) Second, the Kristersson government has overseen a significant drop in gang-related gun violence, a problem that has shaken Sweden in recent years and sailed to the top of many voters’ priorities.

During the election campaign, the left were nevertheless able to capitalise on some of the most egregious effects of these policy changes, including the gratuitous cruelty of deportations in which the children of immigrants with permanent resident permits, who have been raised in Sweden, have received orders to leave the country on the day they turn 18. Many of those who supported tighter controls on immigration did not seem to imagine it would extend to cases like this. But, by and large, the left bloc squandered its lead. The Left was plagued by a scandal over local and regional electoral candidates who posted antisemitic and homophobic sentiments on social media, exposing a lack of basic political discipline and failure of due diligence. And while the Social Democrats campaigned on several popular policies (such as improved affordability, cheaper dental care and better sick pay), they did not always succeed in setting the terms of the debate, and all too often slid into their old habit of warning the electorate of the danger of the far right, including the unthinkable horror of giving the Sweden Democrats ministerial posts. Such warnings made little sense in a context where, as far as the public is concerned, the far right has basically already been in government. In Sweden as well as elsewhere, fearmongering about the far right is no substitute for the articulation of a distinct left-wing alternative.

entry.summary: After a knife-edge election, the left looks set to form a government. But the far right have already transformed the country’s political landscape.

entry.title: Warning from Germany: It’s Socialism or Barbarism

div.p: In just two weeks, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won two state elections, in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, more than doubling its vote share and opening the door to fascist rule for the first time since the fall of the Nazi regime, even if it may fail to secure the necessary support to form a government. Meanwhile, in Berlin, The Left (Die Linke) has scored a stunning victory that should make Elif Eralp the city-state’s first mayor of Turkish origin – in Germany’s capital, home to the world’s largest Turkish diaspora, in which over a quarter of adult residents cannot vote because they are not German citizens.

The Left did best among young voters and in the districts most shaped by migration. Its victory has finally started a countermovement to the AfD’s seemingly inevitable rise, and shown that a progressive majority is possible, in part inspired by Zohran Mamdani and Zack Polanski. The reasons are not hard to see. The Left was the only party to campaign hard on social justice and affordability. As the housing crisis escalated, it pledged to honour Berlin’s popular but contested 2021 referendum to socialise more than 200,000 flats owned by major corporate landlords. Because the plan rests on a rarely used constitutional provision, it is an experiment that could open the way to socialising other basic infrastructure and social goods, forming the core of a leftist political response to the crisis of the present. Crucially, the Left was also the only party to resist the framing of migration as a problem, to insist that antiracism is essential to antifascism, to oppose Germany’s role as Israel’s second-largest arms supplier after the US, and to criticise the genocidal war on Gaza, if not always in those terms.

Its success is all the more striking because it came amid a sweeping political and media campaign painting the party as a hotbed of irresponsible radicals and antisemites. That campaign hit a new low when the CDU’s lead candidate, Stefan Evers, called The Left the party of division because of its ‘hostility to Jews and to landlords’, invoking an antisemitic trope himself (only days after Chancellor Friedrich Merz described antisemitism as a form of hatred of foreigners, symbolically excluding German Jews from the German people). The election has not ended the smear campaign: politicians and mainstream media are already escalating their demonisation, trying to prevent the Left from forming a coalition government. In a situation in which fascist majorities are a real possibility, the centrist merger of a revived Red Scare with open racism should tell you all you need to know about how seriously they mean their anti-fascism. In truth, next to the AfD’s open fascism, the real politics of division has been practised by the CDU – mired in scandals including the misappropriation of funds earmarked for fighting antisemitism – and by the historic centre-left party too, the SPD.

While the political mainstream insists that only the AfD puts society at risk of authoritarian or fascist regression, the last few years say otherwise. The authoritarian turn, which can be understood as a process of fascisation, is enabled by crises internal to liberal democracies: immiseration through declining wages and rising prices, spiralling inequality, the degradation of public infrastructure, a sense that the future has been foreclosed. It is driven not only by the far right’s openly fascist answers to these crises but also by the supposedly liberal centre, which has internalised and normalised new forms of anti-migrant state racism, partly out of conviction and partly out of panic. In trying to weaken the AfD by mimicking it, the centre has predictably only strengthened it.

The parties of the so-called centre (the CDU, the SPD and even the Greens — forget about the by-now-irrelevant neoliberal FDP) have not only committed to austerity and cruelty towards those perceived as socially weak. They have actively undermined or suspended basic norms of the democratic rule of law. They have shown open contempt for international law and human rights, especially when it comes to Israel and the US, restricted freedom of assembly and the right to protest, especially with regard to Palestine solidarity, attacked academic and artistic freedom, and blamed migrants for the crisis and for widespread experiences of decline. The message is twofold. The vision of a free and equal society, however limited its realisation, is passé. And if you are not among those who can hope to make it, the state and the law will not protect you. They will push you out, or keep you down, by any means necessary, including state-led violence.

Instead of treating fascism as the opposite of liberal democracy, we should see fascisation operating within it — or what is left of it — in ways that cannot be pinned on extremists alone. The differences between liberal and fascist regimes are real, but so is fascisation, especially for racialised, excluded and marginalised people. It normalises violence against minorities labelled weak or dangerous. It narrows the space for dissent, whether through the repression of protest or the neoliberal destruction of universities and other spaces enabling critical engagement. And it spreads the sense that preserving what remains of the status quo and its affordances requires abandoning the very idea of a shared future.

Contemporary Germany thus shows two converging modes of identitarian, violent retrenchment. Both retreat from the ground that emancipatory struggles have won over recent decades in broadening access to social and political rights. Both promise, defensively, to secure the material and symbolic privileges of a dominant section of the population in times of decline. The first is explicitly racist: the AfD fixes an exclusionary notion of ‘the people’ and its borders. The second comes from the supposedly liberal centre, in more salonfähig (socially respectable) tones. Here, the defence of a colonial genocide is key to a wider authoritarian turn.

Staatsräson, ‘reason of state’, for Germany officially means fighting antisemitism and supporting Israel. It is presented as a lesson of the Holocaust. In practice it is the latest incarnation of a politics of division and a narrowing of who belongs. By massively expanding and instrumentalising the definition of antisemitism around ‘Israel-related antisemitism’, Staatsräson outsources antisemitism to migrant populations in the discourse of ‘imported antisemitism’ and uses it to attack challenges to the status quo from the post-migrant left. It becomes a tool for securing white dominance and managing the migration society in times of crisis, while maintaining a self-understanding of enlightened civilisational superiority. Instead of confronting real and rising antisemitism, especially on the far right, the hegemonic response targets migrants, the left, and grassroots pro-democracy and anti-racist initiatives, playing into the hands of a repressive, racist project.

It also lets mainstream parties have it both ways. They can position themselves against the AfD, framed as the anti-system option for white voters whose ‘legitimate concerns’ go unheard, while escalating centrist anti-migrant and anti-refugee rhetoric and policies without ceding the moral high ground. The immediate consequence is that people ‘with a migration background’ are subject to constant supervision and disciplining, pushing them out of politics, mainstream media, cultural and academic institutions. ‘Remigration’, the neo-fascist euphemism for mass deportation and ethnic cleansing, is the logical endpoint of this unacknowledged convergence.

The result is the mainstreaming of a politics of enmity, desolidarisation, separation, sacrifice and elimination as the dominant response to today’s economic, ecological and geopolitical crises. The rights, and indeed the lives, of ever larger groups of people — first racialised minorities, increasingly those seen as socially weak or unproductive — no longer count equally, or at all. They are abandoned and brutalised. The message is that this could happen to you if you do not comply with the imperatives of securing the existing order.

header.h2: Who Can Beat the New Right?

div.p: In what they present as a response to the AfD, large parts of the political spectrum feed the very dynamics driving fascisation. First, the centre tails the far-right framing of migration as a problem. Horst Seehofer, then interior minister, called migration ‘the mother of all problems’ after the racist riots in Chemnitz in 2018. Treating migration as the source of the crisis is a gateway for fascisation, both rhetorically and materially: it identifies enemies and builds up a punitive and repressive state apparatus. Meanwhile, attachment to privileges that must be protected at all costs — the project of Fortress Germany and Fortress EU — grows more violent and aggressive as its subjects sense that the promise of liberation and protection offered by the fortress is empty.

Secondly, therefore, the scapegoating logic does not stop with migrants. It extends to other groups branded weak or dangerous, such as trans people and people with disabilities, who are cast as existential liabilities, threats to established claims to wealth, power and identity, and to a presumed right to control the borders protecting these claims. Rather than address real societal challenges, fascisation delivers more of the same: more division, exclusion, disenfranchisement and violence — and so deepens the crisis.

We are witnessing a fight against the multicultural society that already exists. Fascisation is anything but abstract: real people already experience it as concrete violence. The fascist pseudo-response to a misdiagnosed crisis reproduces and intensifies the structural crises and the violence they breed. It converts structural violence into direct violence, terror and domination, against and within the society shaped by migration, in the name of a racially purified ethno-nationalist community. The structural transformation that alone could answer the underlying crisis remains blocked, and the crisis keeps getting worse.

Against the fascist temptation to manage decline to the advantage of the few, a renewed left is the only hope — not only in Germany. And one of the lessons of the last elections here is that the left’s only hope is to insist on the actual possibility of an anti-nationalist, anti-identitarian, anti-fascist and non-capitalist way of living together in solidarity, beyond the destructive zero-sum logic of an economic and civilisational war of all against all that centrists seem unable or unwilling to transcend. If we want any shared future at all, it will have to be radically different from the past and the present.

entry.summary: Fascism is at the door, and liberals are ushering it in. Only the left offers hope.

entry.title: Britain Must Not Join the War on Yemen

div.p: Last night, Andy Burnham announced that the UK will provide ‘defensive air to air refuelling’ support to Saudi Arabia’s military, plunging Britain into another disastrous conflict in the Middle East. Amid a worsening humanitarian situation in Yemen, the latest Saudi attacks risk more civilian deaths and an acute refugee crisis, with thousands already displaced.

Burnham’s arrival in office seemed to suggest the possibility of a break from Starmer’s complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza and collusion with the war on Iran — two shameful stains on Labour’s legacy. But with this new announcement, history seems to be repeating itself.

The conflict with the Houthis began in 2015 when a Saudi-led coalition, backed by the US and UK, intervened in Yemen’s civil war. Their goals were to dislodge the Houthis and to prop up the government headed by Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, who would keep the country in favour with Saudi Arabia. The campaign killed nearly 9,000 civilians, with many more dying from the effects of the war, from collapsed services to starvation to epidemics.

Britain supplied spare parts, ammunition and maintenance to the aggressors along with unconditional political support. The then foreign secretary Philip Hammond declared that the UK would assist the Saudi military ‘in every practical way short of engaging in combat’, which included sending military advisers.

London thus gave the Saudi coalition a free hand to commit a litany of war crimes. As early as 2016, a UN panel found that it had engaged in ‘widespread and systematic’ attacks on civilian targets. In 2018, a Saudi airstrike hit a school bus, killing 29 children. Cluster bombing targeted medical facilities and ancient heritage sites. Yet the onslaught ultimately failed. The Saudis were forced to sign a truce in 2022, but by that time it was too late: Yemen had already been shattered.

The fragile peace was broken after the recent bombing of Sana’a airport by Saudi Arabia. The subsequent Houthi offensive has seen them gain control of Yemen’s western coast and, with it, the chokepoint of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, an area crucial to Saudi Arabian oil transportation.

The UK responded by providing refueling support for US operations against Yemen last year. While Starmer tried to justify these actions as ‘defensive’, the Pentagon itself reported that they had ‘more likely than not’ resulted in the killing of 281 civilians. Human Rights Watch warned that Britain’s involvement in the operation ‘may make them complicit in war crimes’. On 29 April 2025, Starmer took British involvement up a notch, becoming the tenth British Prime Minister to directly bomb Yemen, as RAF Typhoons carried out a joint UK-US strike south of Sana’a.

This was yet another futile operation. Less than a week later, Trump was forced to sign a peace agreement with the Houthis. But the humanitarian impact of this forever war could not be clearer. Around 47 percent of the Yemeni population are currently experiencing crisis levels of acute food insecurity while nearly half of children under five are acutely malnourished, according to the UN. The World Health Organisation observes that the country is already facing ‘multiple concurrent health risks’, including cholera, measles, dengue, diphtheria and trauma. More than 112,00 people have already been internally displaced, with UN agencies warning that they lack the resources needed to support those forced from their homes.

Now, Burnham has agreed that Britain will help to refuel the Saudis’ killer jets — visiting yet more destruction and misery on the poorest country in the region. Outlandishly, he tried to frame this decision as an attempt to alleviate the UK’s cost-of-living crisis, as if deepening civilian suffering in Yemen would somehow offer respite to communities in Britain. If anything, more bombing will only exacerbate the inflationary pressures triggered by Trump’s war on Iran, which are pushing up prices for working-class people worldwide.

When the war on Yemen started in 2015, Labour opposed Britain’s involvement and committed to both suspending arm sales to Saudi Arabia and presenting a resolution at the UN to end the conflict. History now looks kindly on this position.

Burnham should follow this example and break from years of failed international policy. His government could rebuild the international aid programmes that Starmer brutally cut, and provide safe passage to refugees fleeing the war, rather than pouring further fuel into the region.

entry.summary: The Saudis have already inflicted massive destruction on the region’s poorest country. Now, as the humanitarian crisis worsens, the UK government is planning to pour more fuel on the fire.

entry.title: Without Public Ownership, ‘Public Control’ is an Illusion

div.p: Last month, West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker took most of the West Midlands’ buses into public ownership. For £24 million, the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) has acquired National Express’s entire regional operation, taking on their 1,400 buses and responsibility for 94 per cent of local journeys.
Backed by £11.5 million from No. 10 North, this is one of the largest transfers of bus services into public hands since the era of privatisation began.

This is good. For too long, municipal ownership has been treated as an impossibility. Until recently, councils were banned from even setting up bus companies. Only a handful of operators survived Thatcher’s purge, like Nottingham and Reading, and remain in public hands.

But there is a contradiction here. West Midlands Bus Limited, the new publicly-owned company, will ‘not bid for franchised routes’ when bus franchising begins in 2027. It makes the purchase look more like a stopgap, with the mayoralty acting as an operator of last resort until it can find a private company to take it back over.

The circumstances of the sale suggest crisis management more than a commitment to public buses. Mobico, National Express’s parent company, wanted to bail on the region. It openly describes the sale as part of a strategy to ‘monetise’ its bus assets and ‘de-risk’ before franchising came in.

It’s a playbook we’re seeing right across the country. The public carries the risk; private companies take the returns. If the balance sheet is threatened, they leave. Private capital has a strategy for bus services. Westminster needs one of its own.

Franchising has been seen as an answer. In his last job as Greater Manchester Mayor, Burnham made a success of the Bee Network. As Prime Minister, he claims he will place public control at the heart of his vision of ‘Manchesterism’, using it as a lever for economic growth.

In his first speech as Prime Minister, he identified part of what went wrong under Thatcher. ‘Political power was centralised, economic power privatised’, resulting in a ‘failed economic model’ which ‘allows wealth to be extracted and siphoned out.’ His answer is that we need to ‘be relentless’ at giving people and places ‘ownership and control.’

The basic diagnosis is right. But ownership and control are not the same. Franchising gives public authorities control over the network. But the buses are still run by private companies, who make a profit from doing so. Public ownership goes further: money derived from running the service can stay in the service.
We should be relentless about giving communities control. But you cannot truly have control over something you do not own.

The story of bus services over recent decades has been one of managed decline. Bus mileage, the total distance covered by our bus network, peaked around the millennium. By 2014/15, coverage had fallen to 1.29 billion miles; by 2024/25, it was down to one billion. In a decade, the UK lost almost a quarter of its bus network.

Greater Manchester has begun to reverse that decline. Bus mileage increased by 7 percent during the first year of franchising. But restoring a network costs money — and under franchising a large chunk of that is still gifted to private capital rather than being reinvested to improve the network.

Greater Manchester spends £227m each year subsidising its bus network; London spends almost £1.2 billion. There is nothing wrong with investing in public transport, but this isn’t that. More than 40 percent of bus operator revenues come from public subsidy. And when Stagecoach, First, and Arriva still record seven- or eight-figure profits, the limits of franchising become clear: public transport is still being run to generate shareholder profit.

We need a new story to tell. Before Manchesterism, there was the People’s Republic of South Yorkshire. In the 1980s, South Yorkshire understood that public transport could shape a region. In those days public subsidy meant low fares. At 10p for adults and just 2p for children, South Yorkshire’s buses were the envy of the country.

Thatcher declared war on council-owned buses. In 1986 she deregulated bus services, stripping councils of the power to set routes, fares and timetables; and in 1989 her government ordered South Yorkshire to privatise its bus company — or face her Ministers breaking it up by force.

Because South Yorkshire’s bus company was about more than providing a service. It reflected a belief that local government should transform people’s surroundings and raise expectations. Being able to travel, for whatever purpose, without having to spend half your wages or owning a car, changed what people could do with their lives.

It would cost £3 billion per year to make all bus services in England free at the point of delivery. In the context of government spending, that is a small sum to pay to transform how millions of people get around. And considering how much good public transport boosts productivity the economic benefits could easily outweigh the cost.
But doing so would mean recognising that public transport is an enabling service — that it functions, in Mick Lynch’s words, as ‘a tool of liberation’.
This is something that we had once. Something that was taken from all of us. Richard Parker taking the West Midlands buses into public ownership is a brave first step towards getting it back.
But after four decades of decline, we cannot settle for half measures. It is time to put the public back in charge of public transport. We need public ownership now.

entry.summary: The West Midlands has shown that municipal bus companies are possible. So why is it already preparing to hand routes back to the private sector?

entry.title: Agent of Feminism

div.p: Political movements are always defining their boundaries. When someone who acts in the name of an emancipatory struggle does something questionable or even reactionary, a typical response is: Well, they must not be a proper member of our movement, because no real comrade would have done that. There’s nothing wrong with this position, at least at the level of argument. It is typically an attempt to define what the movement should be, how its members should ideally conduct themselves, rather than what it is or has been.

Obituaries of Gloria Steinem, who died earlier this month, can for the most part be divided into two opposite camps. Steinem is seen either as iconic and emblematic feminist, or as the opposite: a false feminist who reflected what are taken to be limitations of the Second Wave, and who may have even betrayed the movement at the behest of the CIA.

Feminism is not an organisation with a membership card. Anyone can claim to be a feminist, though others might disagree. The question is what to do when this disagreement emerges — when we are confronted with those things that would make someone by our (anti-imperialist, anti-capitalist, and so on standards) not meaningfully a feminist. The feminist theorist Sophie Lewis has an answer to this: such people are not not part of the movement, but they are best understood as representatives of ‘enemy feminisms’. They remain ‘feminist’ in the sense of contesting patriarchal constraints, though their politics are not ours.

Gloria Steinem’s name is synonymous with feminism in the US. She was thirty-five — young, but not so young — in the late 1960s, when ‘trust nobody over thirty’ was a popular catchphrase and feminism was an emergent mass movement, part of which had broken off from a huge national mobilisation of mostly young people against a segregationist racial order at home and imperial violence maintained by an overlapping racial order abroad. These movements had made it impossible for things to carry on in the same way.

In 1969, Steinem attended a public abortion ‘speak-out’ on the streets of New York, and, having had an abortion herself in her early twenties, was particularly moved by the collective sharing of experiences that had hitherto been understood as private. Speak-outs formed part of an arsenal of new feminist tactics which sought to politicise women’s experience, advance a theoretical understanding of their oppression and bring them into collective struggle. Women would regularly gather in these public forums and in smaller consciousness-raising groups for lively, intense, serious discussions, often a site of productive disagreements.

Steinem quickly gained a role in the movement that involved popularising feminism among much wider layers of the public, particularly through Ms magazine, which she co-founded in 1972. One of the major dividing lines of that moment was the extent to which women, seeking liberation as women, should work with or in other organisations or strike out alone. Fed up with persistent chauvinism in male-dominated political groups, many had decided it was easier to form their own. Steinem noted that the same women who had been ‘jailed, beaten and Maced side-by-side with their social-activist male counterparts’ would be relegated to ‘typing and making coffee’ within the structures of Students for a Democratic Society.

The rationale for acting autonomously was partly pragmatic: it’s hard to get things done if you’re constantly making the coffee, and what you might want done will now likely have expanded to include overcoming the fact that you’re the person making the coffee. But it was also a political commitment: some feminists — calling themselves radical feminists — saw women’s liberation as a goal that could not be advanced through existing political institutions.

While radical feminists differed on many points, they tended to agree on the following: women’s oppression, which they took to mean men’s direct power over women — exerted particularly through sexuality — is the most important, most structuring, most fundamental power relation. On this view, liberation will come only from women organising autonomously. And because their oppression was believed to predate and form the basis of all other social oppressions, their freedom would result in a larger transformation of society itself.

In one sense Steinem was a liberal who believed in convincing, lobbying and legislating within existing institutions, making particular use of the media to raise issues like abortion, bias against women in the public sphere, equal pay and political representation. Steinem’s solutions to patriarchy were different sex roles and family norms, plus a meritocratic labour market. As Lewis puts it in an incisive obituary, Steinem’s anti-communist strand of feminism had ‘just enough radical credibility’ to divert the energy of social movements towards ‘peaceful electoralisms’.

Yet in another, important sense, Steinem was a radical feminist and saw herself as such, popularising a version of liberalised radical feminism whose diagnoses were radical even if its tactics were not. She saw confronting patriarchy as a collective project (albeit not a revolutionary one) rather than something women could achieve individually. She eschewed the radical-feminist ambition to overturn the entire system while adopting its premise that women are a class oppressed by another class, men, especially through sexuality, and that this oppression was the primary social relation.

Retrospectives on the so-called ‘Second Wave’ are often strangely ahistorical. The typical view is that the feminist movements of the late 1960s to 1980s were insufficiently inclusive, insufficiently attentive to questions of race and class, and that they ultimately failed as a result. Critics tend to think that we can now do things differently with the benefit of hindsight. But the trouble is that feminism was never a unitary movement, especially not over quite so many years, and such criticisms were often made by dissenting feminist currents at the time. (Steinem was in some ways ‘better’ than the standard view of the Second Wave; for her, social and racial equality objectives related to the women’s struggle, and she at least partly recanted her earlier transphobia.)

If there was an overarching problem with the Second Wave, and indeed with the radical feminism that dominated the feminist political landscape particularly in the US, it was that it underdetermined feminist politics. Belief in the primacy of male dominance, its greater salience relative to other relationships of power, is compatible with all kinds of politics, from across the ideological spectrum.

Radical feminists were right to claim that transcending women’s subordination relies on their empowerment. But what tactics make that possible, especially when women (and men) are less united than early slogans like ‘Sisterhood is Powerful’ would suggest? In the revolutionary moment of radical feminism’s formation, the idea was for the autonomous women’s movement to support a general attack on the system, which was seen as verging on collapse. But outside that moment, how should women direct their consciousness of men’s power over them? What does an insurrectionary politics to end women’s subordination look like in practice?

Should you take a legal strategy by overturning laws that disempower women? Or punishing actions that oppress women? Engage in separatism? Attack the symbols of women’s oppression (though how to be sure of what those are)? Overcome sexist problems in public services by coming up with a parallel system of healthcare services or support for women escaping abuse? A broad range of tactics has been used to advance radical feminist goals, many of which are not radical in the sense in which it is generally used — working with the police, creating new laws, becoming embedded in the political establishment through advocacy and charity work. These can and have often ended up with an easy accommodation with the political status quo or even alliances with the political right.

Steinem’s less-than-virtuous associations are well-known, and have often been emphasised by critics on her left. In the late 1950s and early 60s she worked for a CIA-funded research organisation which sent delegations of young Americans to attend the ‘World Festival of Youth and Students’, an event that brought people from socialist, capitalist and Third World countries together in the inhospitable conditions of the Cold War. Her role, according to the Redstockings group of New York feminists, seems to have involved propagandising and allegedly reporting back on attendees.

Steinem’s was a liberal variant of radical feminism, and her views on imperialism were those of the classic American liberal. She was critical of the war on Vietnam and the first Gulf War — seen as blips or excesses of US foreign policy — but she was a lifelong apologist for Zionism who refused to speak out on the genocide in Gaza and in later life committed herself wholeheartedly to the Democratic Party as the agent of progress. Yet to claim that Steinem’s liberal, radical, anti-communist feminism was a product of the CIA would be to ignore fertile soil in which it germinated. The Agency didn’t ‘need’ Steinem to domesticate feminism, nor did she need it to divert revolutionary energies to more reformist ends. The defeat of the feminist project was not just a story of infiltration and betrayal, but of the struggle between its more and less emancipatory tendencies, forced to coexist within the same movement, and even within the same thinkers.

There’s a dynamic here that goes much further than Steinem herself. Feminism, especially feminism that sees its ideal as not that different from the existing world, suffers from a tension between liberation as a collective goal and liberation as an individual state of being. Because there can be a degree of flexibility in expectations of what it means to be a man or woman — as we have seen from the significant shifts in the sixty or so years since the start of the Second Wave — feminism can produce both revolutionary horizons and aspirational totems. Neither is a ‘betrayal’ of the movement; both are reflections of this inherent contradiction.

One might say that the attachment to Steinem as a figurehead of the movement is an index of its unhappy fortunes over the past half-century. If feminism can no longer hope to achieve freedom writ large, then it needs individuals who appear to embody freedom, in however limited a form. If universal liberation is elusive, then the personal escape from oppression — however rare or fleeting — is the next best thing.

A problem with individual feminist change is that it can assume all kinds of different forms depending on what any individual takes ‘liberation’ to mean. Without the presence of political movements or collective, political possibilities, reactionary, non-liberatory accounts of liberation (the Girlboss of the 2010s; the lady War Hawk; ‘choice feminism’) are likely to proliferate, with stupefying and anti-solidaristic effects.

Yet, even so, it remains unhelpful to deny the irreducibly interpersonal aspects of feminism, or to write off the adulation for Steinem as nothing more than a liberal excesses or celebrity fetish. Feminism, on such a view, is only about collective goals, politics with a capital ‘P’. But the fact is that participation in movements, and engagement with their ideas and leaders, can change people in different, more subjective ways: not only in the big sweep of history, but in their ordinary lives.

Today, some of Steinem’s views might look conflicting or incompatible: she opposed the imperialist adventure in Vietnam but aligned herself with the Clinton wing of the Democrats; she professed anti-racism but refused to speak out against the genocide of Palestinians; she demanded better protections for workers but opposed the communist movement that fought for them. Yet these tensions reflect the limits of American liberalism itself, which permits dissent from the established order but only up to a point. Of course, few people are really coherent in their beliefs. And those who are tend to be quite strange. But some inconsistencies are symptomatic rather than singular. Steinem’s speak to the vexed politics of the Second Wave: a site of struggle and contestation in which there were, at least across the course of a lifetime, or the entire spread of a movement, very few coherent or non-contested positions.

The impulse to reduce this to a charge of ‘betrayal’ is driven by an understandable aim to define a movement’s boundaries: what is and is not acceptable within it. But while this might be a useful exercise in ideological discipline, it rarely maps onto the political or historical reality of social movements, whose defeats might teach us something if we looked at them more clearly.

entry.summary: Gloria Steinem is remembered as either an icon of feminism or a traitor to the movement. But her strange blend of liberalism and radicalism reflects the tensions of the Second Wave itself.

entry.title: British Academia is Dying. It’s Time for a National Industrial Response

author.name: Members of the University Rank and File Workers Group

div.p: There is a point at which the crisis stops being an exception. This is now the condition of UK higher education. Across Britain, universities are cutting staff, closing courses, shrinking departments, and tearing up the assumptions on which generations of workers built their careers. It is clear that redundancies are no longer isolated incidents affecting small or financially beleaguered universities. They are spreading into the upper echelons of academic prestige.

Nearly half of UK universities are projected to run deficits in 2026, with up to 50 institutions potentially facing insolvency or closure in the following year. Recently released figures show that for the first time in more than a decade, the number of academic staff employed across UK universities has fallen. The number of job losses in the sector in recent years is estimated to be around 30,000. To put this figure into context: the official number alone is the same as the tally of jobs lost in 1992 with the final closures of deep-pit mines. Meanwhile, private degree delivery centres are fast becoming the only financially viable model in the sector. These catastrophes are the outcome of a structural crisis in the sector’s funding model, as the number of international students, on whom universities rely for tuition fees, has gone into freefall.

The long-term consequences are becoming increasingly clear. A university can cut its way out of a deficit only for so long. At some point, an institution will fail. And when that happens, it will be the result of a funding regime that has transferred risk from the state to individual universities, from universities to workers, and from workers to students. Today, in ever greater numbers, students are refusing to take on that risk.

Contrary to popular understanding, the damage caused by this crisis will not stop at the campus gates. For more than two decades, British governments have encouraged local economies to orient themselves around universities as anchor employers in an increasingly service-based economy. The language of the ‘knowledge economy’ became embedded under New Labour, when universities were cast simultaneously as engines of regional regeneration, suppliers of skilled labour, centres of innovation, and magnets for international investment.

Cities and towns were encouraged to build economic and urban strategies around them. Student accommodation was constructed; retail centres adapted to student populations; housing markets incorporated thousands of renters; local businesses became dependent on university expenditure; hospitals and schools developed partnerships with universities; cultural institutions became conduits for international research communities. In many towns and cities, the university became one of the largest employers and, for better and for worse, one of the few institutions capable of generating sustained economic activity. That model is now being dismantled.

The trajectory of contraction, privatisation and offshoring of higher education is an open secret within the British political establishment. The language of ‘efficiency’, ‘consolidation’, ‘financial sustainability’, ‘internationalisation’ and ‘closing loop-holes on migration’ disguises the more definitive restructuring that’s underway. The sector is being reorganised around expanded provision abroad, a smaller number of institutions at home and a radically reduced domestic workforce. Teaching and research functions, meanwhile, are increasingly exposed to outsourcing, corporate and military interests, international delivery models and technological substitution.

To achieve this structural transformation, the current generation of university senior managers are embarking on a process of educational vandalism. Courses and programmes have been slashed without even basic justifications. Prolific funding generators have been sacked in the name of ‘long-term financial savings’, and legal redundancy consultation processes have been universally flouted. Perhaps the biggest indignity has been the outsourcing of institutional ‘future-proofing’ to management consultancy firms with little or no prior experience of the sector. Frontline staff have been treated as unqualified bystanders rather than precious sources of institutional knowledge and market insight. The result has been the imposition of standardised cost-saving measures targeting the same disciplinary areas, leading to a concentration of competition around a homogenous academic offering.

Despite the scale of the damage, few politicians have dared to ask what happens when the institutions around which entire local economies have been built begin to contract. The answer is already visible in towns and cities where universities are cutting staff and closing courses. Take the closure of the Southend Campus of the University of Essex: the decision, it is estimated, will remove £101 million in direct economic activity from the city, with local businesses already feeling the impact.

The consequences will only cascade. Fewer jobs mean less spending. Fewer students mean less demand for accommodation, hospitality and retail. When a university becomes financially unviable, the economic shock will spread through the community that grew around it. New Labour’s ‘knowledge economy’ was sold as a route out of regional decline. The very real risk today is that the collapse of its economic foundations will simply sharpen it. And with that, the economic and social conditions in which the far-right have prospered will be generalised.

In the face of the most significant attack the university sector has ever seen, how has the largest of the unions in the sector, the University and College Union (UCU), responded? After regular national industrial actions over pay, pay-related issues and pensions during the period of 2018-23, in 2023 the UCU won a significant victory in restoring USS pensions to pre-pandemic levels for pre-92 universities. But on pay and pay-related issues, it suffered a devastating defeat in the Marking and Assessment Boycott (MAB) later that year.

By the end of 2023, UCU members in higher education were demoralised and disorganised, with some members facing extremely punitive pay deductions for taking part in the MAB. Since then, members have been fighting reactively, branch by branch, to stave off redundancies after university managers announce cuts. Vital local fights against cuts have been taking place in the context of an energised student and staff activism, focused mainly on calls for BDS and solidarity with Palestine, but this has not altered the underlying industrial impotence.

In the absence of a national response to the shrinking of the sector, a new organisational current began to take shape across higher education: rank-and-file day schools. Run every other month, these have become laboratories for bringing together workers from different institutions and trade unions, and creating spaces where people can talk about the sector as a whole. The politics is straightforward: workers need to understand the forces shaping their workplaces and their unions if they are going to change them. In order to do this at a sectoral level, they need to talk and organise with other workers outside their own workplaces and union branches.

In the two years they have been running, the day schools have covered how to respond to redundancies, casualisation, outsourcing, industrial strategy, and branch organisation, creating a space for workers to think politically about what universities are for.

At the beginning of 2025, discussions at the rank-and-file day school turned towards the sector’s financial crisis. Based on the harrowing experience of fighting local redundancy campaigns, the questions posed were brutally practical. If the crisis is caused by the funding model, why are workers only fighting its consequences? Why should trade unionists at different universities be engaged in separate struggles against redundancies, when the job cuts are being driven by the same structural pressures? Why not confront the political authority responsible for the system itself? The strategy that emerged was a proposed national trade dispute with the Secretary of State for Education over funding in the sector: the Secretary of State dispute.

For years, sector employers, represented represented by the Universities & Colleges Employers Association (UCEA), had already laid the ground for such an escalation: during national negotiations, they repeatedly claimed that casualisation, workload and equality could not be resolved at the institutional level. As the financial crisis deepened, senior managers and UCEA itself went further, arguing that the underlying funding model was unlikely to change and that redundancies were therefore unavoidable. In other words, these issues could not be resolved by institutions themselves, with meaningful progress instead ultimately requiring state intervention.

Rank-and-file activists then raised money through branches to get legal advice, which corroborated the approach sketched out in the day schools. On the basis of that advice, we developed a motion and took the argument back into branches. In May 2025, the motion was carried at the UCU Higher Education Sector Conference — making the strategy union policy. The resolutions of the motion were clear: to open a trade dispute with the Secretary of State over higher education funding; coordinate the strategy with other higher education unions and students; and campaign around the connection between funding, employment conditions and student experience.

The following day, the Congress resolution and SoS dispute strategy made the headlines. It was said at the time that if the Labour government did not respond to the crisis, the union would have no other choice than to take industrial action against the state. More than a year later and the dispute has not been opened.

Rank-and-file activists are now renewing their organising efforts in response to this delay. Dozens of UCU branches are coordinating to push the Secretary of State dispute back to the centre of the union’s strategic discussions, and have called for an emergency conference to determine the future of its national industrial strategy.

In the coming months, this kind of cross-branch coordination will be needed to restore members’ confidence in the union’s national industrial capacity. Workers in the sector also know that there are no wins on a branch by branch basis. Higher education is a national, and international, ecosystem. In the current regime one department’s closure might feel like another department’s windfall, but the reality is a sector in terminal decline where no worker or student is ‘winning’. Branches need a national fight.

It may seem that now, of all times, is not the right moment to be talking about building rank-and-file structures in the union. But despite the pain inflicted by sackings in the sector, many UCU branches have emerged stronger from local struggles. Branches which had barely any internal infrastructure now have consolidated teams of representatives, regular member meetings, communication channels, casework teams, departmental representatives; they know how to run local ballots and industrial actions, to negotiate with bosses, to listen and mobilise their members and students, and they know their rights and how to use them. In this respect, branches are in a far better position to carry out industrial actions that hold real leverage.

If led by branches, a national industrial dispute with the Labour government over sector funding could harness these energies and give them political direction. A national industrial dispute could be coordinated with other education workers; the National Education Union (NEU) is balloting members at the end of the year in a comparable dispute with the Secretary of State. A window is opening for a major national industrial confrontation over the state of education, the likes of which was never experienced by Keir Starmer, but could seriously test Andy Burnham’s government.

If university workers are to succeed in this strategy, it will need to make clear that the fight over higher education is not only about the jobs and conditions of lecturers. It is also about workers across the university and the local community. It is about our current students and everyone who might want to study in the future.

We believe in universities not just as a vehicle for investment in the so-called knowledge economy, but as parts of a wider social infrastructure, opened up to communities with an expansive conception of education as a common good. Students should be able to learn critical theory and carpentry, programming and anthropology. Cost and the fear of one’s job prospects afterwards should not be the main reason for choosing a course — or not. Winning the Secretary of State campaign will not in itself be sufficient to end the permacrisis of UK Higher Education and transform the sector for the better.
